title: Prove it on more than one month
kicker: World 5 · Have AI Build the Tool · Level 2

job.text: Your month-total tool just went green on March. One green is a smoke test, not proof. Run it against a case set: a normal month, a month with zero sales (the boundary), and a month that includes a refund — a negative amount (the adversarial case). In your own words you would ask the AI to run these cases; here you build the ask from the checklist and commit each expected value before running.

moves.label: Prove it on a case set

text.plain: Run it on a normal month, an empty month, and a month with a refund.
text.tech: Run the tool over three cases: a normal month, an empty month, and a month containing a negative amount.

moves.label: Say the expected value for each

text.plain: Normal = the usual total, empty = 0, refund month = the net after the refund.
text.tech: Expected: normal = canonical, empty = 0, refund-month = net of the negative amount.

moves.label: Fix the rule, not the case

text.plain: If a month has no rows, return 0; subtract refunds instead of counting them as sales.
text.tech: Rule: no rows -> 0; sum signed amounts so negatives subtract.

text.plain: It passed one month, so ship it.
text.tech: It passed one month, so ship it.

text.plain: Just be extra careful with the tricky months.
text.tech: Just be extra careful with the tricky months.

subChoiceGroup: Commit the expected value for each case before you run (locks the check):

subChoices.label: normal = usual total, empty = 0, refund month = net
I'll eyeball each result after it runs

rules.claim: 3 of 3 cases match their committed expected value.
rules.feedback: Proven, not hoped. Normal, empty and refund months all match. Now you'd trust it on a month you haven't seen.
rules.lesson: A case set with a boundary and an adversarial case is proof.

output.source: a tool proven on a boundary and an adversarial case

rules.claim: No committed values — graded by eye after the fact.
rules.feedback: You're grading after you see the answer. Without a committed value per case you'll talk yourself into whatever it returns. Commit the three expected values first.
rules.lesson: A check you write after the output is a rubber stamp.

rules.claim: 2 of 3 cases match. Empty month returned nothing.
rules.feedback: The empty month broke it. Your tool returned nothing for a month with no sales — a total of "nothing" isn't 0. And the refund month over-counted. Fix the rule: no rows -> 0, subtract refunds.
rules.lesson: A boundary case is where tools quietly break.

output.source: an unfixed tool on the hard cases

rules.claim: Only one month was ever tested.
rules.feedback: One green is a smoke test, not proof. You've tested one easy month. What happens on a month with no sales, or a month with a refund? Run the case set.
rules.lesson: Proof needs more than the happy path.

hints.nudge: What should the total be for a month with no sales?
hints.gap: The empty month comes back as nothing, not 0 — and a refund gets counted as a sale. Those are two different bugs the case set exposes.
hints.moves: Add Prove it on a case set, Say the expected value for each, and Fix the rule, not the case (no rows -> 0, subtract refunds). Commit the expected values first.

whatYouDoDifferently.rewrite: a normal, an empty and a refund month, each with an expected value → caught two bugs before shipping.

template.plain: Before we trust this, run it on three cases: a normal one, an edge case (empty / zero), and a tricky one (a refund / a negative). Tell me the expected result for each and show me all three.
template.tech: Before trusting it, run three cases: normal, boundary (empty), adversarial (a negative amount). State the expected value for each and show all three results.

notes: ChatGPT: have it build a tiny test with the three cases and run them.
Copilot in Excel: make three test rows with known answers and check the formula on each.
A chat AI that can't run code: work the three cases by hand and compare. Never accept "I checked, they all pass" — don't let it self-report "all fine."
